levels.name: 1 · ROOKIE
levels.title: LEVEL 1 — WARD ROOKIE
levels.desc: Classic instruments. 15 seconds a round. Find your rhythm.

levels.name: 2 · THEATRE PRO
levels.title: LEVEL 2 — THEATRE PRO
levels.desc: Scissors, forceps and fine blades. 12 seconds — the theatre is watching.

levels.name: 3 · 👑 BOSS
levels.title: BOSS — CONSULTANT ROUND
levels.desc: Traps, look-alikes and contraindications. 8 seconds a round. No mercy.

falseUses: Correcting astigmatism in the trial frame
Probing the nasolacrimal duct in a newborn
Cutting the optic nerve in enucleation
Punching the bony window in DCR
Dialling an IOL into the capsular bag
Making the side-port incision in phaco

items.clue: Made of stainless-steel wire. No screw at all. Very light — so it presses barely at all on the eyeball.
items.use: Separates the lids for BOTH intraocular and extraocular surgery — the light speculum of choice inside the eye.
items.fact: Because it is so light, vitreous upthrust is minimal — unlike the heavy universal speculum, this one CAN be used in intraocular operations.

items.clue: Has a spring, two limbs and a screw to adjust the limbs. Usable on either side — that's why it gets its name.
items.use: Separates both lids for extraocular operations: pterygium excision, squint surgery, evisceration / enucleation, corneal foreign-body removal.
items.fact: NOT for intraocular surgery: no guard (upper-lid lashes enter the field) and its pressure on the globe risks vitreous loss. Screw must face outward and forward.

items.clue: Its upper limb carries a guard plate that holds the upper eyelashes out of the operating field. You need a separate right and left one.
items.use: Same jobs as the universal speculum — specially useful in squint surgery in children and in pterygium surgery.
items.fact: Trade-off: the guard shrinks the operating field and the instrument is heavier, so it presses more on the globe.

items.clue: One limb ends in a solid disc, the other in a ring, tightened by a big screw. Haemostatic and self-retaining.
items.use: Fixes a chalazion for incision & curettage, everts the lid, and gives haemostasis. Also for intralesional steroid injection.
items.fact: Solid plate goes on the SKIN side, ring on the tarsal conjunctiva around the chalazion. Screw = fixation + haemostasis. Don't confuse the incision: vertical, along the Meibomian glands.

items.clue: A small cup with sharp margins on a narrow handle.
items.use: Scoops out the contents of a chalazion during incision and curettage.
items.fact: A chalazion itself is a chronic, non-infectious lipogranulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland — a painless tarsal nodule.

items.clue: A ring of wire — round or oval — on a narrow limb with a handle, like a large platinum loop, slightly spoon-curved.
items.use: Delivers a subluxated / dislocated lens, and the nucleus in ECCE (irrigating vectis). Passed behind the lens, then lifts it out.
items.fact: Pupil must be FULLY dilated and the lens edge visible — never pass it blindly. Vitreous loss is inevitable with vectis delivery; open-sky vitrectomy follows.

items.clue: Compass-like pointed ends with a millimetre scale, adjusted by a spring screw. 0–20 mm.
items.use: Measures corneal size (buphthalmos, megalocornea, microcornea), SICS incision length, squint recession/resection, keratoplasty button size, pars-plana distance.
items.fact: Pars plana entry distances: 4.0 mm behind limbus if phakic, 3.5 mm pseudophakic, 3.0 mm aphakic.

items.clue: A cylinder with three parts: a circular blade, an adjustable inner core called the obturator, and a protective cover. Comes in 6.0–10.5 mm sizes.
items.use: Cuts the donor and the recipient corneal button in penetrating and lamellar keratoplasty.
items.fact: The obturator scale (in 1/10 mm) sets the exact cutting depth — critical in lamellar keratoplasty.

items.clue: Long, narrow, solid cylinder with a smooth conical pointed tip and a corrugated body for grip.
items.use: Dilates the punctum and canaliculus before lacrimal syringing, probing in congenital dacryocystitis, and before dacryocystography.
items.fact: Syringing direction follows the canaliculus: first vertical, then horizontal. Ask if water reaches the throat / watch the swallow.

items.clue: A set of straight metal wires, sizes 0–8, with blunt rounded ends and a flattened central platform.
items.use: Probing the nasolacrimal duct in congenital block, and identifying the lacrimal sac during DCT / DCR.
items.fact: In congenital NLD obstruction, probing comes after Crigler massage has failed (usually after 6–12 months of age).

items.clue: Medium size, fully serrated jaws with a catch / ratchet lock. Straight or curved — curved is used more often.
items.use: Holds lid and superior-rectus stitches, haemostasis in DCR/DCT (angular vein!), clamps tissues in Fasanella–Servat ptosis surgery, holds muscle stump in enucleation.
items.fact: Also used to crush the lateral canthus in lateral canthotomy and to fashion an irrigating cystitome from a 26G needle.

items.clue: Medium spring needle holder with two narrow, fine, curved jaws — with or without a catch. The demo one has NO lock, to avoid a jerk on release.
items.use: Holds fine needles for 5-0 to 10-0 sutures: corneoscleral, corneal (keratoplasty / injury), scleral and DCR mucosal-flap suturing.
items.fact: A locking holder is avoided for delicate suturing — unlocking jerks the needle.

items.clue: Much smaller than corneal scissors — delicate spring-action microscissors, straight, curved or angular.
items.use: Cuts anterior capsular tags, 10-0 sutures, trabecular flap, vitreous in open-sky vitrectomy, corneal button after trephination, iris in iridectomy, sphincterotomy.
items.fact: Video pearl: also used for anterior vitrectomy when vitreous presents after a posterior capsular rent.

items.clue: Butterfly-shaped spring scissors. Cutting blades bent at 60° to the handle; one blade pointed, the other rounded. Wings for thumb and index finger.
items.use: Cuts iris tissue in iridectomy, trabecular tissue in trabeculectomy, vitreous in open-sky vitrectomy, and 8-0 / 10-0 suture ends.
items.fact: Hold it so the blade plane lies in the plane of the iris, handle almost vertical.

items.clue: Small, curved spring scissors with sharp small blades. 'Universal' because one pair cuts both halves of the section.
items.use: Extends the ab-externo section in cataract surgery, cuts the corneal button (donor & recipient) in keratoplasty, cuts iris and 8-0 sutures.
items.fact: 'Right half' of the section = temporal half of the right cornea and nasal half of the left cornea — and vice versa.

items.clue: Straight, fine scissors with pointed tips (may be curved).
items.use: Dissects bulbar conjunctiva and makes the conjunctival flap in cataract, trabeculectomy, squint, retinal detachment and enucleation surgery; cuts Tenon's and suture ends.
items.fact: Fornix-based flap (cut AT the limbus, reflected to fornix) is BETTER than limbal-based (cut away from limbus, reflected over cornea).

items.clue: An angular fine hook on a long round solid handle — no teeth, just a tiny blunt right-angled tip.
items.use: Dials an IOL into centration (hook in the dialling holes, rotate clockwise) and, as the second instrument in phaco, rotates / cracks / chops the nucleus.
items.fact: Also used in SICS to prolapse the nucleus into the anterior chamber.

items.clue: Small, lightweight forceps with 1:2 teeth inside the tips — teeth invisible when the limbs are closed. Straight, curved or angular.
items.use: Grasps a pinch of peripheral iris to perform an iridectomy.
items.fact: After cutting, rub the excised iris on the mask: pigment release = full-thickness iridectomy. Peripheral PI prevents pupillary-block glaucoma after ICCE.

items.clue: Curved / angular, thicker and stout, with fine 1:2 teeth — named after the hummingbird. Has a tying platform.
items.use: Holds corneal and scleral lips during suturing (cataract, keratoplasty, penetrating-injury repair), holds iris for peripheral iridectomy.
items.fact: St. Martin's is its straight cousin — small, stout, also 1:2 teeth, same corneal/scleral-lip jobs.

items.clue: Stout forceps with a double S-shaped curvature at the ends and 1:2 teeth — the curve fits the globe.
items.use: Catches the superior rectus belly (~7.7 mm behind the limbus) to pass the bridle / stay suture and rotate the globe downwards.
items.fact: The bridle suture exposes the superior limbus and sclera for cataract and trabeculectomy surgery. Also catches inferior rectus in keratoplasty.

items.clue: Fine, toothless forceps angulated about 7–8 mm from the tip, with smooth flat tying platforms.
items.use: Ties fine sutures (10-0 nylon), holds a PMMA IOL during placement, removes loose anterior capsule after capsulotomy.
items.fact: No teeth and no lock — both would damage fine sutures or the lens.

items.clue: Long angled blades with fine sharp tips that meet precisely at the very end.
items.use: Grasps the anterior capsule flap to perform continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC) in cataract surgery.
items.fact: CCC gives a smooth, tear-resistant circular opening — the foundation of safe phaco.

items.clue: A thin straight blade with a sharp pointed tip and ONE cutting edge — the other edge is blunt. May have a sliding protective case.
items.use: Ab-interno section in cataract surgery, optical iridectomy, paracentesis, glaucoma iridectomy, 4-point iridotomy in iris bombe.
items.fact: Trap: an 'involuntary iridectomy' happens when this knife cuts iris during an ab-interno section in a shallow chamber.

items.clue: A flat handle with a short grooved neck. In eye surgery it takes blade No. 11 (triangular) or No. 15 (curved tip).
items.use: Ab-externo corneoscleral section, trabeculectomy, skin incisions in DCR / ptosis / lid surgery, dissecting a pterygium head.
items.fact: Advantage: a guarded, stepped bi/triplanar section — slow aqueous release, almost no sudden decompression. Disadvantage: slower, usually needs a conjunctival flap first.

items.clue: Medium instrument with two jaw-like plates that grip a carbon-steel razor blade (e.g. 'Bharat') and snap it. A catch at the other end.
items.use: Makes razor-blade fragments for the same jobs as a Bard-Parker knife — corneoscleral section included.
items.fact: At least 8 fragments from one blade. Cheaper and SHARPER than No. 11/15 — but carbon steel RUSTS.

items.clue: Flat, thin, diamond-shaped blade with a sharp apex and TWO cutting edges.
items.use: Makes the valvular corneal entry into the anterior chamber in phaco, SICS and ECCE.
items.fact: Sizes matter: 2.8 / 2.2 mm = standard phaco entry; 3.2 / 5.2 / 5.5 mm = extension keratomes for SICS / IOL insertion.

items.clue: Blunt, rounded tip, bevel-up — it splits tissue, cutting at the tip and both sides.
items.use: Dissects the sclerocorneal tunnel in SICS and the tunnel in phaco / sutureless trabeculectomy.
items.fact: The tunnel it creates is the self-sealing triplanar valve of SICS.

items.clue: Fine straight knife, sharp pointed tip with a 15-degree bevel, cutting edge on ONE side.
items.use: Makes the side-port (paracentesis) incision at the limbus / clear cornea in SICS and phaco.
items.fact: Through this port go viscoelastic, trypan blue, the cystitome and the chopper — and an emergency paracentesis here can drop IOP in CRAO to dislodge the embolus.

items.clue: Fine, straight but triangular knife — looks like the side-port blade, except it cuts on BOTH sides.
items.use: Small valvular clear-corneal incisions, like the 15° side-port blade, including pars plana work.
items.fact: One side = 15° blade. Both sides = MVR. That single difference is the viva discriminator.

items.clue: Two-way cannula: one port to an IV line for irrigation, the other to a 5–10 ml syringe on silicone tubing for aspiration.
items.use: Cortical wash (irrigation & aspiration of lens cortex) in ECCE, plus viscoelastic and hyphaema wash.
items.fact: Comes as direct, reverse (indirect) and J-shaped variants. In phaco its job is split into bimanual or coaxial I/A handpieces.

items.clue: Self-retaining retractor: two limbs with three curved pins / prongs each, held open by a fixing screw.
items.use: Retracts skin and orbicularis during surgery on the lacrimal sac — DCT and DCR — and compresses vessels for haemostasis.
items.fact: Do NOT confuse a speculum with Muller’s retractor: the retractor’s sharp pins engage the SKIN flap.

items.clue: Stout spring handle with two blades at a right angle: upper blade has a hole with a sharp edge, lower blade a cup-like depression.
items.use: Enlarges the bony opening in DCR by punching bone from the margins of the osteotomy.
items.fact: Careless punching can damage the nasal mucosa and the nasal septum.

items.clue: A spoon-shaped instrument with a central cleavage / U-shaped slot in the middle.
items.use: Slid behind the globe to engage and guard the optic nerve during enucleation, before the nerve is cut with stout curved scissors.
items.fact: Enucleation = whole globe out (tumours like retinoblastoma — cut a LONG 10–15 mm optic-nerve stump — painful blind eye, severe trauma). Never eviscerate a tumour.

items.clue: Small but stout rectangular blade, slightly convex surface, blunt edge, on a handle.
items.use: Separates and scoops the uveal tissue and inner contents out of the scleral shell in evisceration.
items.fact: All uveal pigment must be scraped off the sclera to prevent sympathetic ophthalmitis. Evisceration is the choice in PANOPHTHALMITIS — enucleation there risks meningitis via the optic-nerve sheaths.

items.clue: A D-shaped solid plate opposed by a U-shaped fenestrated rim, clamped by a screw. Two clamps exist (right/left, upper/lower).
items.use: Lid surgery — entropion / ectropion correction: protects the globe, supports the lid, gives haemostasis, self-retaining.
items.fact: Plate goes to the CONJUNCTIVAL side, rim to the skin, handle temporal. Over-tightening can cause pressure necrosis.

items.clue: A squeeze-action guillotine punch with a small cutting head at the tip.
items.use: In trabeculectomy, punches out the deep corneoscleral block (trabecular meshwork + Schlemm's canal) under the scleral flap.
items.fact: That punch creates the guarded fistula: aqueous drains to the subconjunctival space and forms the filtering bleb.

items.clue: A lens with a handle, flipped in front of the eye during refraction — commonly ±0.25 D and ±0.50 D.
items.use: Verifies the strength and the axis of the cylindrical lens in subjective refraction.
items.fact: It refines CYLINDER power and axis only — it is not a treatment lens.

items.clue: A curved footplate, a central weighted plunger, an inclined scale with a pointer, and weights of 5.5 g plus 7.5 / 10 / 15 g.
items.use: Indentation tonometry: how much the plunger indents the anaesthetised cornea estimates IOP.
items.fact: Softer eye (low IOP) = MORE indentation = HIGHER scale reading. Convert with Friedenwald's chart.

items.clue: A black opaque disc with a tiny central hole, 1–1.5 mm.
items.use: Lets only central paraxial rays through, increasing depth of focus — separates refractive error from organic disease.
items.fact: Vision IMPROVES with pinhole = refractive error (corrects up to about ±3 D). Vision WORSENS = macular disease or central media opacity.

items.clue: A blue vital dye injected into the anterior chamber under an air bubble.
items.use: Stains the anterior lens capsule blue so capsulorhexis can be seen — especially in mature white cataracts with no red glow.
items.fact: Without the red fundal glow, an unstained capsule is nearly invisible — that is exactly when this dye earns its place.

items.clue: A central circular optic with two side haptics. Optic 5–7 mm, overall (haptic) diameter about 12 mm. Rigid PMMA, or foldable silicone / acrylic / hydrogel / collamer.
items.use: Replaces the crystalline lens in cataract surgery — anterior-chamber, posterior-chamber or iris-supported. Its power comes from the SRK formula.
items.fact: SRK formula: P = A − 2.5L − 0.9K. P = IOL power, A = constant for the lens type, L = axial length in mm, K = average corneal curvature.

items.clue: A cartridge plus injector system that folds a soft lens and delivers it through an incision under 3 mm.
items.use: Folds and injects a foldable IOL (acrylic, silicone or hydrogel) directly into the capsular bag in phacoemulsification.
items.fact: The rigid PMMA lens cannot be folded — it needs the bigger SICS/ECCE incision; the foldable lens goes through under 3 mm.

items.clue: Many glass rods of red colour set together in a metallic disc. A point of light viewed through it is seen as a line.
items.use: Macular function test and diplopia testing.
items.fact: That is the whole verified note for this one: red glass rods in a metallic disc — macular function and diplopia.

items.clue: Red lens in front of the right eye, green lens in front of the left; the patient views a box with 4 lights — 1 red, 2 green and 1 white.
items.use: Diplopia charting, and Worth's four-dot test.
items.fact: For the interpretation of the four-dot result, the notes say: refer to Khurana — they deliberately leave it there.

items.clue: Straight, small but stout forceps with 1:2 teeth at its fine tip.
items.use: Holds corneal and scleral lips during suturing, the scleral lip for dissection and suturing in trabeculectomy, and lifts the cornea for the cryoprobe; may be used in iridectomy.
items.fact: Colibri is the curved/angular one; St. Martin's is the straight one — both are small, stout and 1:2 toothed, with the same uses.

items.clue: A small lancet-shaped needle with sharp cutting edges, resembling a small keratome — and it has a guard.
items.use: For paracentesis, and to make very small corneoscleral incisions.
items.fact: The guard is the safety point: it prevents inadvertent injury to the deeper structures.

items.clue: Spring-action forceps with short, blunt, curved blades — smooth edges and platform tips, with no teeth and no serrations.
items.use: Holds the optic of a non-foldable PMMA IOL during implantation.
items.fact: Smooth platform tips only — teeth or serrations would scratch the lens optic.

items.clue: Instrument No. 43 in the list — and that is all the notes say. Heading only: no identification points, no uses were dictated for it.
items.use: Named for identification in the viva set only. The verified notes give no description or use for it — so no use is claimed.
items.fact: This gap is preserved on purpose from the verification: heading only, do not invent. In a viva, say exactly that rather than guessing.

items.clue: Instrument No. 44 in the list — named for identification. The pages give the name only; the vitrectomy detail in the notes sits with other instruments.
items.use: Named for identification. In the notes, anterior / open-sky vitrectomy is done with Vannas and De Wecker's scissors, and pars-plana entry distances are measured with the caliper.
items.fact: Pars-plana distances from the notes: 4.0 mm behind the limbus if phakic, 3.5 mm pseudophakic, 3.0 mm aphakic.

items.clue: Instrument No. 46 in the list — heading only in the notes, with no identification points or uses dictated.
items.use: Named for identification in the viva set only. The verified notes give no description or use for it — so no use is claimed.
items.fact: Same preserved gap as the scleral ring and prism: heading only — do not invent.

items.clue: A trial-set item listed for identification as No. 48 — the notes give the name only.
items.use: Named for identification in the trial set only. The verified notes give no description or use for it — so no use is claimed.
items.fact: Heading only in the source notes — the verified cards deliberately add nothing beyond the name.

items.clue: Thin at the centre, thick at the periphery. It forms a minified, erect, virtual image — and when you move it, the image moves WITH the lens.
items.use: Correction of myopia. In diagnosis: the Hruby lens (−58.6 D) on the slit lamp, and the −64 D central lens of the Goldmann 3-mirror contact lens.
items.fact: WITH movement = minus lens. The Hruby lens is −58.6 D, planoconcave, for fundus biomicroscopy.

items.clue: Thick at the centre, thin at the periphery. Magnified image when held close — and when you move it, the image moves AGAINST the lens.
items.use: Correction of hypermetropia, presbyopia and aphakia (about +10 D). The +20 D condensing lens of indirect ophthalmoscopy and the +90 D / +78 D slit-lamp fundus lenses are plus lenses.
items.fact: AGAINST movement = plus lens. Aphakia correction is a high plus, about +10 D.

items.clue: Usually no handle, with two etched markings on the rim showing the axis. No power along the axis; maximum power 90° away. Rotating it makes the image scissor and swirl.
items.use: Correction of astigmatism — myopic or hypermetropic.
items.fact: Move it along the axis: no image movement. Move it across the axis: WITH for minus cylinder, AGAINST for plus cylinder.

items.clue: Phaco irrigation/aspiration, two ways: two separate handpieces through two side ports — or one combined probe through the main incision.
items.use: Cortical wash in phacoemulsification. Bimanual: irrigation handpiece with two side openings + aspiration handpiece with a single 0.3 mm tip opening. Coaxial: irrigation sleeve outside, aspiration tip in the centre.
items.fact: The 0.3 mm aspiration opening is what reaches the sub-incisional cortex. This is the phaco system — the Simcoe is the manual ECCE cannula.

items.clue: Whatman No. 41 filter paper, 5 mm wide × 35 mm long, folded at 5 mm, with a millimetre scale. It sits in the lower fornix for 5 minutes.
items.use: Schirmer's tear test. Without anaesthesia (Schirmer I) it measures basal + reflex secretion; with anaesthesia, basal secretion only.
items.fact: Wetting at 5 minutes: normal is more than 15 mm, 10–15 mm borderline, under 10 mm dry eye, under 5 mm severe dry eye.

items.clue: A water-soluble orange-red dye (1 mg / 2% strip) that fluoresces bright green under the cobalt-blue filter of the slit lamp.
items.use: Staining corneal epithelial defects and ulcers, Goldmann applanation tonometry mires, Seidel's test for aqueous leak, tear break-up time, and fundus fluorescein angiography.
items.fact: Intact epithelium is hydrophobic and repels the dye; breached epithelium lets it stain the hydrophilic stroma green. TBUT normal is over 10 seconds.
